questions.question: What general rule does the chapter give for choosing an algorithm to solve a problem?
gold_points: We should prefer an algorithm that is easy to understand, implement, and document.
When performance matters, we must also consider speed and efficient use of computing resources.
Algorithm choice balances understandability with performance concerns.
gold_source: Section 3.1 What This Chapter Is About, PDF page 1 (book page 89)

questions.question: Why is simplicity important when choosing an algorithm for long-term use?
gold_points: A simple algorithm is easier to implement correctly than a complex one.
It is less likely to contain subtle bugs that appear later on unexpected inputs.
A simple algorithm is easier for other people to understand and maintain over time.
gold_source: Section 3.2 Choosing an Algorithm, PDF page 2 (book page 90)

questions.question: How can good documentation help when an algorithm is not very simple?
gold_points: Good comments and documentation can partially compensate for a lack of simplicity.
Clear explanation makes the algorithm easier for a reasonably intelligent reader to understand.
Documentation helps later modification and maintenance by other programmers.
gold_source: Section 3.2 Choosing an Algorithm, PDF page 3 (book page 91)

questions.question: Besides running time, what other resources may a program need to conserve?
gold_points: The amount of storage space used by variables.
The amount of traffic generated on a computer network.
The amount of data moved to and from disks.
gold_source: Section 3.2 Choosing an Algorithm, PDF page 2 (book page 90)

questions.question: Why does the chapter treat running time as the main efficiency concern for large problems?
gold_points: For large problems, running time determines whether a program can practically be used.
Other resources can matter, but running time is the dominant concern in this chapter.
Program efficiency is taken mainly to mean time as a function of input size.
gold_source: Section 3.2 Choosing an Algorithm, PDF page 2 (book page 90)

questions.question: Why are understandability and efficiency often in conflict when choosing algorithms?
gold_points: Algorithms that are efficient for large amounts of data are often more complex.
More understandable algorithms can be slower.
The merge sort versus selection sort comparison illustrates this tradeoff.
gold_source: Section 3.2 Choosing an Algorithm, PDF pages 2-3 (book pages 90-91)

questions.question: Why does the chapter say simplicity is subjective but efficiency is objective?
gold_points: Simplicity depends on whether readers can understand the explanation and code.
Good explanation can improve perceived simplicity.
Efficiency is objective because a program takes the time it takes, leaving no room for dispute.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 3 (book page 91)

questions.question: What are the two principal approaches to summarizing program running time?
gold_points: Benchmarking is one approach.
Analysis is the other approach.
The chapter emphasizes algorithm and program analysis.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 3 (book page 91)

questions.question: What is the purpose of benchmarking when measuring program performance?
gold_points: Benchmarking uses a small collection of typical inputs.
These inputs are treated as representative of the job mix.
A program that performs well on benchmarks is assumed to perform well more generally.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 3 (book page 91)

questions.question: Why should benchmark inputs be representative of the job mix?
gold_points: Benchmarking relies on the assumption that the chosen inputs reflect typical real work.
The benchmark is used as a stand-in for all inputs.
If the inputs are not representative, good benchmark performance may not reflect true overall performance.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 3 (book page 91)

questions.question: Why might a sorting benchmark include empty, singleton, or already sorted lists?
gold_points: These are special input cases worth checking for correctness and efficiency.
Some sorting algorithms behave poorly on already sorted input.
A useful benchmark should cover more than just ordinary random cases.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 3 (book page 91)

questions.question: What does profiling tell us about a program?
gold_points: Profiling helps determine where a program spends its time.
A profiler associates each statement with the fraction of total time spent there.
Profiling helps identify performance hot spots.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 4 (book page 92)

questions.question: What is a statement counter, and how does it differ from a profiler?
gold_points: A statement counter records how many times each statement executes on given inputs.
A profiler focuses on the fraction of total running time spent at each statement.
Both help analyze behavior, but one counts executions while the other emphasizes time.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 4 (book page 92)

questions.question: What is the 90-10 rule in program performance?
gold_points: Most running time is often spent in a small fraction of the source code.
Informally, about 90% of the running time may be spent in 10% of the code.
This reflects locality in where computation time is concentrated.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 4 (book page 92)

questions.question: Why does the 90-10 rule suggest optimizing hot spots rather than the whole program equally?
gold_points: Improving the code where most time is spent yields the biggest overall speedup.
Eliminating time in cold code has little total effect if that code uses little time.
Profiling helps reveal which parts are worth optimizing.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 4 (book page 92)

questions.question: How is the size of a program input chosen during analysis?
gold_points: Inputs are grouped by size before analysis.
The definition of size depends on the problem being solved.
Examples include number of items to sort, the dimension n of an equation system, or some relevant input quantity.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 4 (book page 92)

questions.question: What does the function T(n) represent in running-time analysis?
gold_points: T(n) represents the number of units of time taken on an input of size n.
It is called the running time of the program or algorithm.
It may be interpreted as operation count or time on a standard machine.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF pages 4-5 (book pages 92-93)

questions.question: What does it mean for a program or algorithm to be linear time?
gold_points: Its running time has the form T(n) = cn for some constant c.
Its running time is linearly proportional to the size of the input.
The growth in time matches the growth in input size.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 4 (book page 92)

questions.question: How does the chapter define worst-case running time?
gold_points: Worst-case running time is the maximum running time over all inputs of size n.
It is used when running time depends on the specific input, not only input size.
It gives an upper-bound style summary of performance for size n.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 5 (book page 93)

questions.question: What is average running time, and what important assumption does it usually make?
gold_points: Average running time averages performance over all inputs of size n.
It can be more realistic in practice than worst-case in some settings.
It usually assumes inputs of size n are equally likely, which may not be true.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 5 (book page 93)

questions.question: Why can a linear-time algorithm become preferable to a quadratic-time algorithm as input size grows?
gold_points: A quadratic algorithm can be faster for small inputs because of constant factors.
As input size increases, the slower growth rate of the linear algorithm gives it an increasing advantage.
The running-time form ultimately determines how large a problem can be solved.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 6 (book page 94)

questions.question: Why do faster computers often increase the advantage of lower-growth-rate algorithms?
gold_points: When computers speed up, algorithms with lower growth rates can handle much larger inputs.
The improvement in solvable problem size is greater for slow-growing running times.
Thus hardware improvements can magnify the value of good algorithms.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 6 (book page 94)

questions.question: Why does the chapter reject the claim that better hardware makes algorithm efficiency unimportant?
gold_points: Demand for computational resources keeps growing.
People have made that claim for decades, yet hard problems remain.
Algorithmic efficiency still matters because larger and harder tasks continue to appear.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 7 (book page 95)

questions.question: Why is the transcript-processing example a case where huge efficiency gains may matter less?
gold_points: Its input size is limited by real-world factors such as number of students and classes.
A faster computer does not necessarily make the school process ten times more data.
So speedup may reduce waiting time without changing the problem size much.
gold_source: Section 3.3 Measuring Running Time, PDF page 7 (book page 95)

questions.question: Why is it usually hard to predict the exact running time of a C program in seconds?
gold_points: Running time depends on the machine used.
It also depends on the compiler and generated code.
Even with those known, predicting the exact executed instruction count is often too complex.
gold_source: Section 3.4 Big-Oh and Approximate Running Time, PDF page 8 (book page 96)

questions.question: Why does the chapter use big-oh notation instead of exact time formulas?
gold_points: Big-oh hides constant factors tied to compilers and machines.
It lets us ignore unknowable or unimportant implementation constants.
It still captures the important growth behavior of running time.
gold_source: Section 3.4 Big-Oh and Approximate Running Time, PDF pages 8-9 (book pages 96-97)

questions.question: What are witnesses in a big-oh proof?
gold_points: Witnesses are specific values n0 and c used to prove a big-oh relationship.
They show that T(n) <= c f(n) for all n >= n0.
A proof works by exhibiting witnesses and verifying the inequality.
gold_source: Section 3.4 Big-Oh and Approximate Running Time, PDF page 9 (book page 97)

questions.question: Why can constant factors and low-order terms often be ignored in big-oh expressions?
gold_points: Multiplying by a positive constant does not change big-oh class.
For polynomials, the highest-order term dominates growth for large n.
Low-order terms can be dropped because they grow more slowly than the dominant term.
gold_source: Section 3.4 Big-Oh and Approximate Running Time, PDF pages 10-11 (book pages 98-99)

questions.question: Why is O(n^2) preferred over O(n^3) when both are technically true upper bounds for the same program?
gold_points: We generally want the tightest big-oh upper bound we can prove.
O(n^2) is stronger and more informative than the weaker statement O(n^3).
A preferred bound should also be simple, often with a single term and coefficient 1.
gold_source: Section 3.5 Simplifying Big-Oh Expressions, PDF pages 14-16 (book pages 102-104)

questions.question: How does the chapter estimate the running time of a simple for-loop?
gold_points: First bound the time spent in one iteration of the loop body.
Then multiply that per-iteration bound by the number of iterations.
Initialization and one extra test are low-order O(1) terms that are often neglected.
gold_source: Section 3.6 Analyzing the Running Time of a Program, PDF pages 23-24 (book pages 111-112)
